ratings.comment: Directly lets users leave the kitchen and be alerted; very plausible but an incremental, fairly obvious substitution of the bell.
Reduces interaction and works with walk-away use, but does not address being notified at completion or mobility directly.
Remote viewing supports mobility, though it requires attention to the screen and the camera must survive heat and steam.
Wild and radical, but a battery-powered, mobile magnetron cart is impractical (high power draw, safety) and it is not a cheaper or simpler substitution.
Auto-presenting door is a nice touch but the user still must be near to collect food and it does not notify, so mobility benefit is modest.
Gas/steam sensing for doneness is plausible and gives continuous feedback, though mapping VOCs to a doneness percentage is unreliable across foods.
Acoustic pop detection works well for popcorn and is plausible for other foods, but generalizing is hard; it also directly signals readiness.
A thermochromic film on the door glass would not reliably reflect food temperature, since glass stays cool and the pigment is exposed to the cavity, so the feedback is weak.
An IR array that ends cooking at target temperature is feasible and useful, but the title mismatches the content and it is a known approach.
BLE phone alerts are easy and extend notification range, but they only relay the timer end rather than sensing true doneness, and they are not radical.
Practical and cheap BLE haptic alert that frees the user to leave, but it is a fairly obvious smart-appliance notification and not very radical.
Remote monitoring is common, and remote start does not work without someone loading the food; a smart plug switching a magnetron is also questionable for safety.
Wildly radical and fits the brief, but a ceiling-hung self-propelled microwave raises serious safety and cost problems and is not a cheaper substitution.
Scent as an end-of-cycle signal is novel and cheap, but scent dispersal is slow, imprecise and lingers, and it would mix with food smells.
A robot arm retrieving the food removes the need to be present at the end, but the food would sit and cool, and the arm is complex and costly relative to the problem.
Closed-loop VOC sensing of doneness directly serves the need and is plausible, though the sensors are noisy and must cope with steam, humidity and RF in the cavity.
A projected overlay is flashy, but the doneness data has no source, and a projector near the cavity is impractical, so it shows status without sensing food state.
A steam whistle is a simple, cheap mechanical cue tied to real food temperature, but the vent geometry is awkward and it works only for foods that steam.
A load cell is feasible and cheap, and mass loss is a reasonable moisture proxy, but it is an indirect measure of doneness and varies by food.
A haptic knob is very feasible and helps accessibility, but it only changes how the end alert is delivered and is not radical.
A self-moving oven that brings the food is wild and serves mobility, but the mains cord, hot surfaces and spills make it hard, and it is not really a cheap substitution.
Magnetron current sensing is a plausible, cheap way to end cooking automatically, though it only partly addresses mobility and accuracy of inference is doubtful.
A cheap RF haptic fob is very feasible and directly frees the user to leave, but it is a fairly obvious idea (pagers and restaurant buzzers already work this way).
Barcode-read cook programs are feasible and concrete, but they mainly reduce setup effort, and the user still has to be at the oven to load the food.
A drone carrying hot food is highly radical and relevant, but it is impractical and unsafe, and it is neither cheaper nor simpler.
Novel smell-based done cue that replaces the bell, but heat-rupture capsules are single-use, can't be timed to the end of the cycle, and may leave scent in food or cavity.
Steam/VOC sensing already exists in sensor-cook microwaves, so it's plausible but not radical, and it gives a real readiness signal.
ITO film for shielding and a thermal colour map is intriguing, but ITO's shielding is weak at 2.45 GHz, it would heat in the field, and the display claim is vague.
Thermopile array with phone alerts is feasible and relevant, but it adds cost rather than substituting something cheaper, and the germanium window is questionable.
A piezo haptic knob is simple and accessible, but it only works if the user is touching the knob, so it's a limited readiness cue.
A steam whistle is a plausible, cheap audible cue, but it signals steaming rather than readiness, many foods don't steam, and a vent whistle in a microwave is awkward.
Thermochromic ink is cheap and feasible and shows temperature, but it is visual only and the plate may not match food temperature or be seen from across the room.
Magnetron load sensing is a real idea, but the signal is weak and unreliable for judging doneness, and it is not a substitution for a cheaper part.
A passive clicking bimetal disc gives a direct, powerless ready signal, but metal in a microwave risks arcing and the disc must be placed correctly in the food.
A progress tone from cavity resonance is very novel and informative, but the microwave-frequency resonance is not acoustic, so the mechanism is physically implausible.
Radical and truly substitutive (no added hardware), but magnetron load-pulling signals are noisy and unlikely to give a reliable doneness estimate across foods.

Weight loss is a real moisture proxy and strain gauges are concrete, but a load cell in a rotating roller ring inside a microwave cavity is awkward and mass loss is a weak doneness cue for many foods.
Acoustic boil and sizzle detection is plausible and gives a real-time cue, though a microphone must survive the cavity's heat, steam and RF.
A MOX sensor in the vent is cheap and workable, but the aroma signal is slow, varies by food, and can't sense doneness in many microwave tasks such as reheating.
A passive, zero-power colour indicator is simple, but door glass temperature lags and poorly reflects food state, so it is a weak readiness signal.
Reflected-power sensing is real and plausible, though it is hard to map to doneness reliably, and it addresses end-of-cycle detection more than feedback to the user.
MOX VOC sensors are cheap and already used in some ovens, and aroma peak is a sensible doneness cue, but it is not strongly radical.
A mechanical haptic cue is a simple and accessible substitute for the bell, but it is only felt when the user touches the knob, and cam-driven buzzing is vague.
A thermochromic dot on the vessel gives direct, visible feedback from across the room, which is clever and feasible, though it requires special consumable vessels.
A thermal heat map is highly informative, but a germanium window with a microwave mesh is costly and contradicts the cheaper-substitute goal.
Closing the loop on the food's own state is attractive, but primary current barely tracks food dryness and varies with line voltage, so detection would be unreliable.
Acoustic boiling and popcorn detection already exists in commercial microwaves, but a cavity-wall MEMS mic is plausible, though it must survive heat, moisture and RF.
It reuses the existing motor at no added cost, but the jolts are weak and easy to miss, and they could disturb the food or spill liquid.
A passive thermochromic tray is simple and clever, but it shows tray temperature rather than doneness and lags the food, and the coating must survive washing.
Humidity and VOC sensing in the exhaust is workable and used in some ovens, but it is noisy across foods and the metal-oxide sensor drifts.
A wearable buzzer for end-of-cycle is practical and directly frees the user from standing by, but it is a fairly obvious idea.
A scent alarm is quirky and distinctive, but smell dispersal is unreliable and slow, and it may annoy colleagues in an office.
Remote app control is feasible and relevant, but it is common smart-appliance functionality and not really a substitution; remote start also needs food loaded.
A portable heating puck is radical and enables mobility, but it replaces the microwave itself, and battery induction heating with wireless power transfer is weak for cooking performance.
A team-chat notification is easy and useful, but it is incremental, and a shared channel is noisy and less personal.
Using reflected power as a doneness proxy is clever and uses existing hardware, though the signal is noisy and varies by food, so reliable doneness inference is hard.
Colour sensing with an LED ring is plausible and gives glanceable feedback, but browning only applies to some foods and steam and splatter can interfere.
A readout overlaid on the door window serves feedback well, but a transparent display that survives the microwave environment and keeps shielding intact is technically difficult.
Scent cues are an inclusive, non-auditory signal, but cartridge consumables, lingering odours and unreliable timing make it a weaker fit.
A passive steam whistle is cheap and simple, but it only signals boiling, not general readiness, and the microwave's vent design and noise make it questionable.
Practical and directly frees the user from waiting, but wearable alerts for appliances are already common, so it isn't radical.
Remote control and monitoring via app already exist on smart microwaves, and the brief doesn't need the cam-knob premise, so it's low in novelty but very feasible.
Ultrasonic beacon decoded by phones is somewhat unusual and serves shared kitchens, but phone-side decoding is awkward and a plain push notification would do the job.
A robot that ferries food is radical and fully removes the trips, but it is costly and complex, and not a cheaper substitution.
Scheduled cloud cooking removes attendance, but food loading and pickup logistics are unresolved and it shifts the problem to a service model.
Listening to steam and popping sounds is a clever, plausible state-based doneness signal, though noise from the magnetron, fan and turntable complicates it and the substitution framing is loose.
A VOC sensor in the vent path to detect the aroma plateau is plausible and matches how people judge food, though MOX sensors are slow and food-specific calibration is hard.
An LED colour ring driven by an IR thermopile is feasible and readable across the room, but it is an incremental, fairly obvious idea and surface temperature is a weak doneness proxy.
Haptic and wearable alerts are easy to build and reach users out of the room, but they only signal the timer ending, not real food state, and the idea is common.

A camera with browning detection gives a direct view of the food and is technically possible, but it is already known, costly, and not a simplifying substitution, and it works poorly for non-browning foods.

Passive color cue is appealing, but thermochromic film on the cavity wall or turntable would mostly reflect the plate or wall temperature rather than the food surface, and it would not survive repeated heating and spills well.
A steam whistle gives continuous audible feedback driven by the food itself, but the cavity must be sealed and vented in a safe way, and the sound varies a lot between foods.
A MOX sensor reading VOCs is a real approach already used in some ovens and it directly tracks progress, though the 'scent-release bar' is odd and the readings are noisy.
A transparent shielded door helps visibility, but ITO-style coatings already exist for shielding and this is not a radical idea, and without a light source the interior is dim.
A cavity camera with a phone alert is plausible, as similar products exist, and it serves the need for feedback well, but it adds cost and complexity rather than substituting something simpler.
A wrist buzzer replaces the bell and frees the user to leave, but it is a familiar wearable-alert concept and not radical.
NFC tags set cook programs cheaply, but NFC needs proximity so it is not truly remote, and the mobility benefit is indirect.
A gas sensor for auto-stop does let the user walk away, though MOX sensing of doneness is unreliable and sensor-based doneness detection already exists.
A radical self-driving microwave that brings food to the desk meets the brief's wildness, but safety, a battery-powered magnetron and cost make it barely plausible.
A badge-access heating locker with chat notification is a creative, feasible reframing that frees users from waiting, though it replaces rather than simplifies parts.
A remote cavity camera with near-IR lighting is plausible and lets users watch food from another room, though cameras in microwaves already exist and the solid door change is a modest substitution.
An NFC package tag sets the program automatically, which is feasible and useful, but a metal cavity complicates the antenna and it needs packaging adoption.
A wireless end-of-cycle notification replacing the mechanical bell is cheap and highly feasible, but it is already common in smart appliances and not radical.
A self-driving pod is wildly radical and does serve mobility, but 1 kW inductive transfer, hot-food spills and safety make it barely feasible.
Reflected-power doneness detection automates the endpoint so the user can leave, which is plausible but unreliable across varied foods.

Sensing doneness from popping and sizzling sounds directly answers the need for feedback on food state, but sound classification is unreliable for most foods and the cheap-mic claim ignores the processing cost.
Steam and VOC sensing is plausible, and some microwaves already use humidity sensors, but it is less novel and a single LED ring is a weak feedback channel.
Using reflected RF power as a food-state sensor is clever and radical, but a coupler on a magnetron is hard to implement and temperature estimates would be noisy.
A passive bimetal pop-up flag is simple and tactile, but it detects cavity temperature rather than food state, and mounting it in a rotating hub is awkward.
A BLE ready alert is highly feasible and extends reach, but it is a common, incremental idea that tells the user only that the timer ended, not that the food is ready.
A scent alert reaches the user in any room, which serves mobility well, but it is a one-shot, imprecise signal and a capsule needs replacing each use.
Doneness sensing from reflected power lets the user walk away and is plausible, though accuracy is limited and sensor-based auto-cook already exists.
Far-field voice control is feasible and widely available, but it only sets the cycle remotely and gives no completion alert or food handling.
A self-driving microwave is wild and on-brief, but it is impractical and unsafe with hot food, and it adds cost rather than simplifying.
A battery-powered solid-state microwave frees the user from the socket, but battery power for full-power heating and GaN cost are major hurdles.
Practical and cheap substitution of the bell with a wearable alert, but fairly obvious and not radical.
Wildly radical ceiling-rail applicator, but impractical for safety, leakage, cost, and it does not really free the user from tending the food.
Feasible smart-microwave features that enable remote operation, though the concept is common and not very radical; the door opener adds little.
Robot courier fully removes the need to go to the appliance and is bold, but it is costly and complex, and not a simpler or cheaper substitute.
Whole-home cues and a camera view serve mobility well; scent release is a quirky touch, though the camera in a microwave cavity faces heat and RF challenges.
Closed-loop aroma sensing truly tells when food is done, though gas sensors in a microwave cavity face humidity, RF and contamination challenges.
Acoustic doneness detection is proven for popcorn and is plausible, but it generalizes poorly to other foods and the microwave's own noise interferes.
Passive colour feedback is simple, but the film on the door mesh would not track food temperature well and may degrade or get contaminated.
Phone notifications are feasible and useful but already exist and only report time or temperature, not true readiness, so the idea is not radical.
A haptic knob is cheap and feasible and adds an accessible channel, but it only works if the user is touching the knob, which limits its usefulness.
Primary current sensing is cheap, but it likely correlates weakly with done-ness and is noisy, so it is a plausible but unreliable proxy.
A load cell under the turntable is feasible, though it must cope with the rotating plate and the microwave environment, and mass loss is a reasonable proxy for doneness.
Aroma microcapsules are novel and reach people in other rooms, but they are consumable, hard to control and mismatched to the food, and they add flavor to it.
Acoustic emission is a clever way to sense cooking state, but a piezo on the cavity wall is exposed to heavy noise and RF, and sound classification is hard.
A haptic pulse on the door is simple and feasible, but it only helps if the user is touching the door, so it is a weak notification channel.
Directly frees the user from standing by via remote alert and is very buildable, but wearable and phone notifications for appliances are already common and not radical.
Imaginative robot tray, but a motorized wheeled carrier operating inside a microwave cavity is hard to make safe and heat-proof, and it only partly addresses not having to stand by.
Voice control from another room serves mobility and is plausible, though it is common and it doesn't help with loading food.
Truly radical self-moving microwave that comes to the user, but inductive power at microwave wattage and a mobile hot appliance are impractical and unsafe, and it is not a cheaper substitution.
Gesture door opening is hands-free but still requires being near the oven, and claims of radar sensing through the cabinet wall and opening from across the room are shaky.
Practical and cheap wearable alert that frees the user from standing by the oven, but smartwatch notifications for appliances are already familiar.
Remote start and timer via an app is already on the market, so it is highly feasible and relevant but not radical, and it adds cost rather than simplifying.
A wild, radical idea that fully removes the need to stand by the oven, but it is hard to make safe and reliable with hot food, a microwave cavity and a battery robot inside it.
Using the mains wiring as a chime channel is a clever substitution that works across a building, though powerline signal reliability and noise in the microwave are concerns.
Remote food-state sensing helps users know when to return, but a thermopile on the door has to deal with steam and shielding, and it adds complexity instead of substituting parts.
Using magnetron load response to infer doneness is plausible in principle and serves the need directly, though the signal is noisy and varies widely across foods.
Microwave-excited electrodeless lamps exist, but a bulb in the cavity would see mostly load-independent field and is a weak, ambiguous progress indicator.
Acoustic doneness detection is plausible for popcorn and boiling, though a general classifier is hard and the microphone must survive the cavity.
A heat-triggered scent is a quirky multisensory cue, but capsules are single-use, vent temperature is a poor doneness proxy, and the cue is neither timely nor repeatable.
A susceptor-driven thermochromic label is feasible and gives direct feedback on the food, though it needs special packaging and is not a true substitution for the window.
Practical and cheap, directly frees the user from waiting, but wearable alerts are an obvious, incremental idea.
Remote viewing is feasible and useful, though it still encourages watching rather than truly freeing the user, and the camera adds cost.
Wildly radical and on-brief, but a self-driving microwave carrying hot liquids with leakage risk is impractical and not simpler or cheaper.
Cordless operation is novel but only loosely tied to not standing by the oven, and 700 W resonant transfer and battery supply are hard.
Remote start and auto-door are plausible and relevant, though food must still be loaded by hand and remote microwave operation raises safety concerns.
Passive colour ring is clever and cheap, but it measures the turntable temperature rather than the food, and an irreversible ink works only once and can't be reset.
Acoustic end-of-sizzle detection is intuitive and novel, but a piezo in the RF cavity is hard to make work, and most foods don't crackle.
Vapour sensing already exists in commercial sensor-cook microwaves, so it is plausible and relevant but not very novel.
A probe gives direct and reliable doneness feedback, but it is a well-known approach and not radical.
Reflected-power sensing is highly novel and cheap in principle, but the signal is weak and ambiguous as a doneness indicator.
Acoustic doneness sensing directly addresses real feedback, and popcorn sensors already prove the concept, but calibrating across foods is hard and the title's "sound-free" is confusing.
A cheap, simple and plausible direct visual doneness cue, though it needs a special dish or label and its relation to the SUBSTITUTE operator is loose.
Replaces the lamp with glowing walls, which only helps visibility, not true readiness feedback, and EL film inside a microwave cavity is doubtful.
A concrete load-cell mechanism, but mass loss is a weak proxy for doneness and the turntable load cell is mechanically awkward.
A gas sensor triggering the bell is a novel, food-driven signal, but the aroma peak is unreliable and the sensor needs ventilation.
Reflected-power sensing is physically grounded and uses existing hardware to infer doneness, though the signal is noisy and varies with food type and load.
Acoustic cues like popping are proven for popcorn and a MEMS mic is cheap, but it works only for foods that make distinctive sounds.
A haptic knob is a novel feedback channel and good for accessibility, but it conveys time more than true doneness and a magnetic-particle brake adds cost.
A chipless resonant tag giving core temperature is radical and highly relevant, but it needs a disposable consumable and a reliable in-cavity RF readout, which is hard.
Exhaust gas and humidity sensing is plausible and gives real progress cues, but metal-oxide sensors drift and the signal is indirect.
Practical and cheap substitute for the bell that frees the user, but it is an obvious wearable-notification idea with little radical novelty.
Wild and highly novel, but a mobile robot carrying hot liquids and replacing the turntable is costly and unsafe, and it is not a cheaper substitute.
NFC tap-programming is plausible and replaces the knob, but tapping the coaster still requires being near the microwave, so mobility is only partly served.
A cavity camera with remote monitoring is feasible and lets users stay informed away from the kitchen, though it adds cost rather than simplifying.
The scent and smart-home alert is creative and reaches the whole space, but scent delivery is unreliable and slow, and the ready-signal is vague.
Zero-hardware doneness inference from magnetron load is attractive, but the load-change signal is weak and varies a lot by food type, so reliability is doubtful.
A piezo listening to popcorn-style acoustics is proven, and a rising-pitch progress cue is a clear improvement on a single ding, though it works better for some foods than others.
Thermochromic ink is cheap and passive, but it senses plate temperature rather than food temperature, can degrade over time, and is hard to see in the cavity.
A haptic handle helps accessibility, but it only works if the user is touching the handle, and a MOX sensor is a crude proxy for doneness.
It is very radical, but it needs special containers, the resonators must survive the cavity's RF field, and the oven must read them, so it is hard to realize and unlikely to be adopted.
Remote camera view lets users leave the room and check progress, feasible with shielded mesh ports, though cameras in microwaves already exist and heat/steam are challenges.
Simple, highly feasible BLE wearable alert directly frees the user to roam, but it is incremental and not radical.
Fiber-optic core probe with auto-stop removes the need to monitor; feasible and concrete, though probes exist in ovens and the user must insert one.
A self-driving battery microwave pod is wildly radical but impractical and unsafe (hot liquids, battery power for magnetron), and not really a cheaper substitution.
Motorised RF-choke conveyor hatch is inventive, but the fridge hopper and food loading are unrealistic and safety/cost are hurdles.
Practical and highly feasible, but wearable alerts are an obvious, existing approach and not radical.
Wildly novel mobile cooking pod that delivers food, but shielding, safety and mobile RF emitters make it very implausible.
Concrete mechanism, but it mainly removes stirring and does little for mobility; a ceiling-mounted emitter has safety and complexity issues.
Voice control is already available on commercial microwaves, so it is feasible but not novel, and it still requires loading food at the appliance.
Self-heating sachets are real, but drone delivery adds cost and impracticality, and it effectively abandons the microwave.
Directly solves the need for mobility with proven wearable haptics, but it adds parts rather than substituting cheaper ones and is a fairly obvious idea.
A clever zero-cost substitution that reuses the fan, but the signal only carries within earshot, so it does little for mobility.
Remote time entry by scanning the pack is plausible and concrete, but it addresses only setting the time, not being alerted at the end, and needs a connected oven.
Dose-based cooking by energy is a novel replacement for the cam timer, but its link to mobility rests on app control that is tacked on.
A webhook that posts to a chat channel works anywhere and is easy to build, but it is an obvious IoT notification and adds cost instead of substituting.
Directly frees the user from standing by the oven and is very feasible, but wearable alerts on appliances are already common and not radical.
NFC auto-programming removes the need to set the oven, but the user still has to come back at the end, so it only partly addresses mobility.
Auto end-point sensing already exists in sensor-cook microwaves, and it stops overcooking but gives no notification, so the user may still hover nearby.
A radical delivery robot that brings the food to the user fits the brief, but hot liquids, safety and the cost of a mobile magnetron are major hurdles.
A warm locker with QR unlock lets the user collect on their own schedule, which is plausible for shared offices, though it adds hardware and is more an add-on than a substitution.
A wrist band that buzzes at cycle end is highly practical and directly frees the user, but it's an obvious idea (smart appliance notifications already exist) and a substitution only in a loose sense.
A motorised drawer presenting food is concrete, but the RF choke seal on a sliding drawer is hard, and it only partly addresses the need to be away from the oven.
Phased-array feeds replacing the turntable are real, specific technology, but they remove stirring rather than the need to stay nearby, so the link to mobility is weak.
IR sensing with auto-stop lets the user walk away and is plausible, though sensor cooking already exists in commercial ovens.
A radical, memorable roaming oven that fits the 'wild' brief and the mobility need, but the battery draw for a 700 W magnetron plus safety concerns make it barely feasible.
Highly relevant and easy to build, but wearable alerts for appliances are already common, so it is not radical.
NFC packs simplify setting the program, but the user still has to stand at the oven to tap and load the food, so mobility gains are small.
A shared heating locker with scheduled heating frees the user from waiting, but it changes the product category and covers only a narrow use case.
Remote viewing helps monitoring, but it adds a camera while removing the lamp, which is not a true cheaper substitution, and it does not alert the user.
A radical robotic tray with SLAM is very novel, but it is impractical and costly, and the user still has to load and retrieve food.
Solid-state RF is a real substitution of the magnetron, but magnetron warm-up is only about a second, so the time saved is minimal.
NFC-to-cook is easy to build and removes setup steps, but similar scan-to-cook concepts already exist and it is an addition rather than a substitution.
Sensing the frozen fraction to end defrost automatically saves re-runs and checking, though reliable sensing in a varied cavity is difficult.
Electronic field steering replaces the turntable and heats more evenly, but it saves little time directly and needs multiple solid-state sources.
Susceptor browning is proven and feasible, and it saves a pan or oven step, but it is not a radical idea and does not speed up cooking itself.
Solid-state RF with beam steering and sensing is a real, plausible direction that speeds cooking and removes timing, though cost is high.
Dielectric sensing for auto-stop is plausible and useful, but the 'door latch' title is mismatched and the idea is incremental.
Parallel cooking saves batch time, but sharing one RF source through a switched waveguide manifold splits power, so the time saving is questionable.
A projected guide helps multitasking, but 'holographic' is overstated and it does little to shorten cooking itself.
Phone and NFC control is easy to build but common, and it saves only seconds of setup; remote start also needs the food loaded already.
ITO-coated glass for RF shielding is plausible (similar to existing coated shields), but the mesh holes aren't a major leak source and the electrochromic/lamp claims are muddled.
A touch-free door release and a piezo chime are feasible, but the pinch hazard is minor and a proximity sensor must not replace the mechanical interlocks.

Solid-state RF with a low-voltage bus really does remove the 4 kV shock hazard and is actively being developed, though it is costly, and the title (inductive power transfer) doesn't match the content.
Live leakage sensing with automatic shutdown directly targets radiation safety and is practical, though it is more an addition than a substitution.

A cool, sealed, non-conductive shell addresses burns and shock, but the polymer shell conflicts with the need for RF and EMC shielding, and heat pipes alone are likely insufficient for magnetron cooling.
Ultrasonic thawing is real, but it needs liquid coupling and a plate in a microwave cavity is awkward, and it adds cost rather than substituting something simpler.
Dielectric/RF sensing of thaw state is plausible and useful, but it improves control more than speed and is only moderately radical.
A passive eutectic gel base gives limited heat and conflicts with microwave fields, so it is unlikely to defrost faster.
Water immersion thaws quickly in practice, but pumps, a heated reservoir and water inside a microwave are messy and complex, and the idea departs from substituting simpler parts.
A see-through door barely affects defrost speed, and the claim that it speeds defrosting is unfounded.
Microwaves have essentially no warm-up lag, so the premise is flawed, and heat stored in the base would not speed up reheating of the food.
A camera that detects doneness could prevent re-heating, but it adds cost rather than substituting something simpler, and it only indirectly speeds up reheating.
Solid-state RF is real and offers better control and even heating, but it costs more, which cuts against a cheaper-substitute operator.
Simple and cheap and it replaces the mechanical bell, but it does little for reheating speed.
A stirrer replacing the turntable is an established, plausible substitution that cuts cost, though it gives only modest speed gains.
Solid-state RF is real and exists in niche products; it offers control and reliability, though the claim of faster heating is overstated and the cost is high.
Reflected-power sensing is plausible and helps avoid overcooking, but reflection is a weak proxy for temperature, so accuracy is uncertain; the piezo chime is trivial.
Phase-steered multi-feed heating needs solid-state sources and is credible, and it improves evenness, but it is not much faster and depends on idea 1's technology.
NFC plates are easy to build and save setup time, but they require special plates, and the microwave-safe tag must withstand the field.
A hands-free door is feasible and convenient, but it barely shortens reheating time and adds cost and complexity.
Solid-state phased-array heating is real and substitutes the magnetron, with even, controlled heating that helps nutrient retention, though the health link is indirect and the cost is high.
Microwave steam cooking directly serves nutrient retention and fat-free cooking and is plausible, though steamers already exist and it is not very radical.
Combination microwave-grill/IR browning is established and cuts oil use, but it adds a heater rather than substituting anything and is not very novel.
Camera plus VOC sensing for doneness prevents overcooking and nutrient loss and is plausible, though it is costly and hard to make robust.
Inverter power supplies already exist in microwaves, and the idea has only a tenuous link to healthy diet.
Superheated steam browning without oil is plausible and serves low-fat cooking, though it adds complexity and cost rather than simplifying, and steam crisping is limited.
Sealed steam vessels already exist and retain nutrients well, so it is practical but not radical.
Dielectric doneness sensing is plausible in concept, but reliable in-cavity permittivity measurement is hard and the nutrient link is indirect.
A simple drain rack reduces fat modestly and is easy to build, but is incremental and has a limited effect in microwaves.
Transparent conductive door shielding is a real concept, but it barely serves the healthy-diet need and microwave doors already use metal mesh.
Solid-state RF is real and offers higher efficiency and control, though 700 W GaN cost is high and the efficiency gain over a magnetron is modest, but it directly targets energy use.
Sensing doneness avoids overcooking and removes the lamp draw, but the savings are modest and the idea is not truly a cheaper substitute.
Physically plausible, but 5-10 W recovered is tiny, and the fan is only a small share of use, so the net saving is marginal.
Phased feeds can even out heating and remove the motor, though the motor's draw is already small and the solid-state sources needed add cost.
Creative load matching, but a sliding divider adds complexity, risks RF leakage and cavity detuning, and doesn't truly simplify the product.
Plausible cost-saving motor substitute, but it only addresses evenness indirectly, not defrost speed, and cooling airflow may not give reliable torque.
Load-based end-of-thaw detection directly targets defrost quality, though the sensing signal is subtle and may be noisy in practice.
Susceptor plates are real and could add bottom heating, but conductive heating of a frozen block is slow and it adds cost rather than substituting.
Reusing waste heat is clever, but 40-60 C air adds little thaw speed and adds duct complexity.
Cheap and workable replacement for a cam timer, but it only automates pulsing and does not speed up defrost.
Solid-state RF heating is real and removes the kV rail, though cost and power levels are challenging and the 48 V claim is plausible but not fully proven for household power.
Capacitive controls are plausible but only marginally address the shock and radiation risks, and the gesture and voice framing doesn't match the described elements.
ITO-coated glass is a real RF-shielding concept, but microwave-grade attenuation, durability under heat and the door seals are doubtful, and mesh already contains radiation well.
A simple and highly feasible fail-safe for the capacitor hazard, though it is an incremental addition rather than a radical substitution.
A phase-change liner could limit exterior burns, but its capacity is limited, microwave exteriors are generally not very hot, and the real burn risk lies with the heated food.
Directly solves hot-milk endpoint control and boil-over, though IR temperature sensing in microwaves is a known idea and cup emissivity and window issues add some difficulty.
A real substitution (solid-state RF for the magnetron) that is plausible and concrete, but it only loosely serves the milk need through faster start and safety.
A cute, cheap readiness cue, but steam venting from a closed microwave is unreliable and a whistle does not control heating or prevent boil-over.
